title: On the Rainy River
author: Tim O'Brien
source: The Things They Carried (1990) / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt
citation: O'Brien, Tim. 'On the Rainy River.' The Things They Carried, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 1990, pp. 37–58.

sections.heading: On the Rainy River (Complete Narrative Selection)

epigraph.quote: I survived, but it's not a happy ending. I was a coward. I went to the war.

paragraphs: This is one story I've never told before. Not to anyone. Not to my parents, not to my brother or sister, not even to my wife. To go into it, I've always thought, would only cause embarrassment for all of us, a sudden tightening in the room, but for more than twenty years I've had to live with it, feeling the shame, trying to push it away, and now by putting it down on paper, I'm hoping to relieve at least some of the pressure on my chest.

In the summer of 1968, the month after graduating from Macalester College, I was drafted to fight a war I hated. I was twenty-one years old. I was young, politically naive, yet I knew enough to know that the Vietnam War was wrong. My heart wasn't in it. In college I had taken a stand against the war, attended rallies, signed petitions. The draft notice arrived on June 17, 1968, a damp Friday afternoon. I remember the smell of ink on the envelope.

All that summer I worked as a declotter in an Armour meatpacking plant in my hometown of Worthington, Minnesota. It was gory, soul-deadening work, removing blood clots from the necks of slaughtered pigs with an eight-foot water gun. At night I drove aimlessly around town, feeling an overwhelming dread. I felt paralyzed, caught between the certainty of war and the terrifying shame of running away to Canada.

In mid-August, the paralysis broke. One morning I left a note on the kitchen table, threw some clothes into a bag, and drove north toward the Canadian border. On the afternoon of the second day, I turned off onto a gravel road and arrived at the Tip Top Lodge, a broken-down set of tourist cabins on the edge of the Rainy River, which separates Minnesota from Ontario.

The lodge was run by an old man named Elroy Berdahl. He was eighty-one years old, skinny and shrunken, with sharp blue eyes. He didn't ask questions. For six days, Elroy gave me shelter, food, and chores, letting me chop wood and wash dishes without pressing me about who I was or why I had come to the boundary of the world.

On the final afternoon, Elroy took me out onto the Rainy River in his small aluminum boat to go fishing. The autumn air was crisp. As he cut the motor, the boat drifted into the current, twenty yards from the Canadian shoreline. Canada was right there—a dense wall of spruce and pine. All I had to do was leap from the boat and swim. Freedom was that close.

And right then, I began to weep. A hallucinatory chorus of people appeared along the shorelines: my parents, my hometown neighbors, the town cheerleaders, historical figures, soldiers, politicians, all watching me. I wanted to jump. But a terrible, suffocating embarrassment seized my chest. I couldn't bear the thought of being called a coward, a traitor, a sissy. My whole life seemed to depend upon avoiding the ridicule of people whose values I despised.

Elroy turned the boat around and headed back toward the American shore. He never said a word. The next morning I left a few hundred dollars on the counter, packed my bag, and drove south toward home. I went to the war. I was a coward. I went to the war.
